wine.name: Vouvray Le Haut-Lieu
wine.sites: Le Haut-Lieu, the domaine's first vineyard and its home, bought in 1928: deep clay and limestone, richer than the soils of its other two vineyards, which gives a softer, more open wine than theirs.
wine.making: Each of the three vineyards is made apart, and in a rich autumn the pickers pass through the rows more than once. Whole bunches go to the press uncrushed, and the fermentation runs as long as the richness of the juice demands. The year's ripeness, not a recipe, sets the style: sec, demi-sec or moelleux.
wine.glass: Quince, pear and green apple over lime blossom, beeswax and wool, with a chalky edge; taut as a sec, rounder with a touch of honey as a demi-sec, and always driven by high acidity.
wine.ageing: Bright and open young, it may close for a few years in its middle age and then keeps for decades; the sweet years last half a century.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius for the sec and demi-sec, a little cooler for a moelleux; decant a young sec for half an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The vineyard, a lieu-dit of Vouvray, not an appellation of its own.
Dry: the style the year gave this bottling; another year the same vineyard may be demi-sec.
Medium dry, its sugar balanced by the high acidity of Chenin Blanc.
Sweet, made in rich years from late passes, some berries touched by noble rot.

records.table: Le Haut-Lieu is the first vineyard of Domaine Huet, bought in 1928: Vouvray Chenin Blanc from deep clay and limestone, made dry, medium dry or sweet as the year allows. Quince, pear and beeswax ride on high acidity, so read the label for the style.
records.story: Domaine Huet began in 1928, when a Paris bistro owner whose health had been broken in the First World War came to Vouvray with his son, Gaston Huet (1910 to 2002), and bought Le Haut-Lieu, the first of its vineyards. Taken prisoner in the Second World War, Gaston spent five years in Oflag IV-D, a prison camp in Germany. In 1947 he was elected mayor of Vouvray, an office he held until 1989, and that autumn he made a Haut-Lieu Moelleux that became a Loire wine of history. The domaine took on the walled Clos du Bourg in 1953 and bought Le Mont in 1957, and from then on made each of its three vineyards apart, dry, medium dry or sweet as the year allowed. His son in law joined in 1971, took charge of the cellar in 1976 and turned the vineyards to biodynamic farming at the end of the 1980s. Gaston Huet died in 2002, and in 2003 the domaine passed to the Hwang family, the son in law staying in the cellar until 2012. Le Haut-Lieu, the first of the three, is the plainest lesson in Chenin: one vineyard, one grape, and the year deciding whether the bottle is dry or sweet.

others.name: Vouvray Le Mont
others.note: Bought in 1957, on stony green clay; the most tightly wound of the three vineyards.

others.name: Vouvray Clos du Bourg
others.note: The walled vineyard the domaine took on in 1953, on thin soil over the rock, giving its most concentrated sweet wines.

others.name: Vouvray Pétillant
others.note: Traditional method sparkling Vouvray, aged long on its lees.

traps: Sec, demi-sec and moelleux are styles the year decides, not tiers of quality or of vineyard.
Huet's Pétillant is traditional method sparkling Vouvray, not a pétillant naturel.
Le Haut-Lieu, Le Mont and Clos du Bourg are lieux-dits of Vouvray, not separate appellations.

cards.back: Le Haut-Lieu, bought in 1928, then the walled Clos du Bourg, taken on in 1953, and Le Mont, bought in 1957.

cards.back: The year and the picking: the ripeness and the share of noble rot in each harvest set the style.

questions.exp: He was elected mayor in 1947, and that year's Haut-Lieu Moelleux is a Loire wine of history; 1928 is the founding, 1957 the purchase of Le Mont and 1989 the year he left the mayor's office.

wine.name: Coulée de Serrant
wine.classification: An appellation of its own within Savennières, held whole by one estate
wine.sites: A steep, walled slope above the north bank of the Loire near Angers, thin soil over tilted red schist and quartz facing south and south east, under vine since monks planted it in 1130.
wine.making: Hard pruning keeps yields low, and the grapes are picked by hand in three to five passes over three to four weeks. They ferment slowly with the yeasts of the place, for two to four months or longer, never chaptalised. The wine is raised on its lees, stirred and never racked off, in barrels of 500 litres with almost no new oak, and bottled dry with little or no filtration.
wine.glass: Bruised quince, camomile and beeswax over dried apricot, honey and wet stone, dry despite its honeyed scent; broad and powerful, with high acidity, a gentle bitterness and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Closed in its first five years, when the estate asks for a bottle to be opened a day ahead, it opens with age and is made for long keeping; an opened bottle often tastes better on its third or fourth day.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, as the estate asks, never fridge cold; open a young bottle a day ahead or decant it more than once; a wide white wine glass.

label.means: The appellation of this one walled vineyard, inside Savennières, held whole by a single estate.
The wider appellation of Chenin on schist near Angers, with two named crus inside it, each an appellation of its own.

records.table: Coulée de Serrant is one walled slope of Chenin Blanc above the Loire, planted by monks in 1130 and an appellation held whole by a single estate. Farmed biodynamically since 1981, it is dry yet tastes of honey and quince; open a young bottle a day ahead.
records.story: Cistercian monks planted the slope in 1130, as the estate tells it, on schist above the north bank of the Loire near Angers, and it has been under vine ever since. The writer Curnonsky (1872 to 1956), born in Angers and elected prince of gastronomes in 1927, counted its wine, by the estate's account, among the five great white wines of France. In 1962 a Paris surgeon bought the estate with the Clos de la Coulée de Serrant. His son came home in 1977 after six years as an investment banker in New York and London and, having read Rudolf Steiner (1861 to 1925), whose lectures of 1924 began biodynamic farming, farmed the Coulée biodynamically from 1981 and the whole estate from 1984, an early convert in France. He became a voice for the method, writing books on it that were published in several languages. Because one estate holds the whole appellation, Coulée de Serrant is one of very few French appellations that is also a monopole. On a list it is the wine to explain Savennières: dry Chenin of great power, with an argument about farming in every bottle.

Savennières is dry Chenin; Coteaux du Layon, across the river, is sweet.
Roche aux Moines is a separate named cru next door, not a part of Coulée de Serrant.

wine.name: Pouilly-Fumé Silex
wine.appellation: Pouilly-Fumé; Vin de France since the late 2010s
wine.sites: The domaine's old, low yielding parcels on silex, the flint stones in clay found mostly around Saint-Andelain, which give the wine its name and much of its smoke.
wine.making: Yields are kept low. The juice is fermented and raised in oak barrels of several sizes, among them the long, narrow casks called cigares, of the founder's design, which give the wine more contact with its lees. New oak, a large share in the early years, was cut back over time, to about a quarter by 2002, and the wine rests on its lees for months before bottling.
wine.glass: Gunflint, struck match and smoke over grapefruit, lemon zest and white peach, with a little acacia; dense and long, with high, ripe acidity and a stony, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first five years, it then opens and keeps for fifteen to twenty, far longer than most Sauvignon Blanc.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white Burgundy glass rather than a narrow one.

label.means: The appellation for Sauvignon Blanc around Pouilly-sur-Loire; never Pouilly-Fuissé, the Chardonnay of the Mâconnais.
The flint clay soil the vines grow on, not the name of a vineyard.
Printed in place of Pouilly-Fumé since the late 2010s, when the domaine began to bottle Silex outside the appellation.

records.table: Silex is Didier Dagueneau's Pouilly-Fumé from flint soils around Saint-Andelain: Sauvignon Blanc from low yields, fermented in barrel and rested on its lees. Gunflint and grapefruit lead, and it ages like a white Burgundy rather than a crisp Sauvignon.
records.story: Didier Dagueneau (1956 to 2008) was born at Saint-Andelain into a family of growers, but before wine he raced motorcycle sidecars and drove sled dogs. In 1982 he set up an estate of his own rather than join the family's. Pouilly-Fumé was then often a thin, grassy white, made in steel and bottled early, and he set out to show what the place could give. He cut yields hard, spoke out against neighbours who overcropped, and raised his wines in oak, a large share of it new at first, with long, narrow casks made to his own design. The flint parcels gave Silex, the bottle that made his name, and beside it came Pur Sang and Buisson Renard, and in the far south west a sweet Jurançon, Les Jardins de Babylone. On 17 September 2008 he died when his microlight crashed near Cognac, and his son took the domaine on. Since the late 2010s the domaine has bottled Silex as Vin de France, outside the appellation, though it comes from the same flint. Silex is the bottle that proves Sauvignon Blanc can age: a Loire white to set beside a grand cru Chablis, never a crisp glass for the terrace.

wine.name: Saumur-Champigny Le Bourg
wine.sites: A small parcel of old vines near the village of Chacé, on limestone over the tuffeau, the soft white chalk of Saumur.
wine.making: Picked by hand, the grapes are made in the estate's old cellars cut into the tuffeau. Le Bourg is raised for eighteen months to two years in new oak barriques, where Les Poyeux goes to barrels a year old from Bordeaux châteaux and Le Clos to older wood, and it is bottled without fining or filtering.
wine.glass: Raspberry, black cherry and violet over graphite, tobacco leaf and a little cedar, the green pepper of Cabernet Franc held in check; fine, firm tannin and a long, silky finish.
wine.ageing: Firm when young, it needs ten years and keeps for twenty and more; old vintages take on the silk of mature Burgundy.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The appellation for red wine, mainly Cabernet Franc, from the villages south east of Saumur.
The name of the parcel, a single old vineyard, not a village or a rank.

records.table: Le Bourg is Clos Rougeard's old vine Cabernet Franc from Chacé in Saumur-Champigny, the one red of the estate raised in new oak, for up to two years. It shows raspberry, graphite and silk, and wants ten years in the cellar before it is poured.
records.story: The Foucault family worked vines at Chacé, south east of Saumur, for generations, a line usually traced to 1664, on limestone over the tuffeau whose cellars run beneath the village. While much of Saumur-Champigny was a light red to drink young, the family kept slower ways: picking by hand, long ageing in barrel and bottling without fining or filtration. Two brothers of the family ran the estate for decades and gave its three reds their shape: Le Clos, the estate wine, raised in older barrels; Les Poyeux, the perfumed parcel on sandier soil, in barrels a year old bought from Bordeaux châteaux; and Le Bourg, the old vines, in new oak for eighteen months to two years. One of the brothers died in December 2015, and in 2017, after months of reports, the family sold the estate to the Bouygues family, who already owned Château Montrose in Saint-Estèphe. Le Bourg is the bottle that showed Loire Cabernet Franc could be laid down beside Bordeaux and Burgundy, and the reference point for the Loire reds that followed.

others.name: Saumur-Champigny Les Poyeux

others.name: Saumur Blanc Brézé
others.note: Chenin Blanc from the limestone hill of Brézé, fermented in barrel.

traps: Le Bourg and Les Poyeux are separate parcels, not a village and a cru above it.
Saumur-Champigny is a Cabernet Franc appellation, not a Cabernet Sauvignon one.
Brézé is a hill and a commune of Saumur, and its wine is a white Saumur, not a Saumur-Champigny red.

wine.name: Sancerre La Moussière
wine.sites: Domaine La Moussière, the family's home vineyard on the slopes just west of the hilltop town of Sancerre, facing south and south west, on marl over Kimmeridgian limestone.
wine.making: The biodynamic grapes come from low yields and are picked by hand. The wine is fermented partly in oak barrels, new ones among them, and partly in vats, and kept on its fine lees for several months, which gives it more weight than most Sancerre, before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Grapefruit, white peach and lemon zest over flint, chalk and a little blackcurrant leaf; fuller than most Sancerre, with fresh acidity and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and open within two years of the vintage, it keeps well for five to eight.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass with a tulip bowl.

label.means: The appellation of the hills around the town: white from Sauvignon Blanc, red and rosé from Pinot Noir.
The family's home domaine beside the town, a vineyard name and not a classified cru.
The name of the house, carried by the eldest son of each generation since the nineteenth century.

records.table: Sancerre with more weight than most, La Moussière is Alphonse Mellot's home domaine beside the town: Sauvignon Blanc farmed biodynamically, fermented partly in oak and given months on its lees. It has grapefruit, white peach and flint; serve it cool, not icy.
records.story: The Mellot family traces its records as growers and merchants at Sancerre to 1513, and its history tells of an ancestor whom Louis XIV (1638 to 1715) chose in 1698 as an adviser on wine. Early in the nineteenth century an Alphonse Mellot opened an inn in the town, where he poured the local wines, and by family custom the eldest son of each generation has carried his first name since, so the name on the label has passed from father to son for two centuries. The heart of the estate is Domaine La Moussière, the vineyard on marl over Kimmeridgian limestone just west of the town, and its Sauvignon Blanc carries the name. Where most Sancerre is made in steel to be drunk young, the family farms biodynamically and ferments part of its white in oak before months on the lees. Beside it the family bottles an old vine white, Cuvée Edmond, a selection named Génération XIX for the nineteenth generation, and Pinot Noir from single parcels, which shows Sancerre as a red appellation too. La Moussière is the family's signature on a list: a Sancerre with weight and length, a corrective to the steel bright picture of the appellation.

La Moussière is the domaine's vineyard name, not a classified cru: Sancerre has none.
Sancerre makes red and rosé from Pinot Noir too, so ask which colour a guest means.

cards.front: Why do so many generations of this Sancerre family carry the name Alphonse Mellot?
cards.back: By family custom the eldest son of each generation takes the first name of the Alphonse who opened an inn in Sancerre early in the nineteenth century.

questions.q: A guest likes Alphonse Mellot's La Moussière and asks for the red of the same appellation. Which grape will it be?
questions.exp: Red Sancerre is Pinot Noir; Cabernet Franc makes the reds of Saumur, Chinon and Bourgueil, and Côt is the Touraine name for Malbec.

questions.q: By its own account, since which century has the Mellot family made wine at Sancerre?
questions.exp: The family dates its records to 1513, in the sixteenth century; an ancestor is said to have been chosen by Louis XIV as an adviser on wine in 1698.

report: Rechecked with four searches on 12 November 2026 (one restricted to the family's own domain returned nothing), and one on Louis XIV's dates; the facts beyond the library rest on two secondary sources each, listed in reviews/recheck-loire.json.

Kept La Moussière as the pick: merchants call it the family's flagship vineyard and the domaine carries its name; the library calls Cuvée Edmond the white flagship, and the integrator may weigh Edmond, the prestige old vine white.
The ancestor of 1698 is named César Mellot in the trade's pages; he is described, for want of his dates, and the inn's founder too.
The year the family turned to biodynamics was not found and stays out; the heads of the family of these years are living and are not named outside the house's own name.
